beats.intro: Chapter two, lesson one. What proteins are, and what they do. [[shelf]]Look at an egg, a glass of milk, a handful of beans. Then think of your own hair, your nails, your skin. All of these are made largely of proteins. [[card]]In chapter one we met the amino acid card: one amino acid, with its amino group, its carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a side chain R, all on the alpha carbon. [[line]]Now the amino acids stop standing alone. They line up and join into a chain. And that chain is a protein.
beats.make: [[atoms]]A protein is an organic, complex compound that contains nitrogen. It is made of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and some proteins also contain sulfur. The nitrogen comes from the amino group of every amino acid. [[poly]]Proteins are polymers, which means long chains of repeated units. The units are amino acids, and a chain of amino acids is called a polypeptide. [[core]]One small warning. Later lessons will show proteins that also carry phosphorus, or metals. So treat carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen as the core of every protein, not as the whole story.
beats.peptide: [[two]]How do two amino acids join? Here are two amino acid cards. On the first, look at the carboxyl group. On the second, look at the amino group. [[meet]]The carboxyl group of the first unites with the amino group of the next. It gives up an O H, the amino group gives up a hydrogen, and together they leave as water. [[water]]So one water molecule is released. [[bond]]What remains is a link between a carbon and a nitrogen: C O, N H. This is the peptide link, also called the peptide bond. [[again]]A third amino acid joins the same way, at the free end of the chain, and every join releases one more water.
beats.count: [[tally]]That gives us a rule to count with. Four amino acids joined in a row have three peptide links, and three molecules of water have left. One link fewer than the amino acids. Two amino acids make a dipeptide, three make a tripeptide, and many make a polypeptide. [[undo]]And the reaction can run backwards. Add water, with acid or an enzyme, and each peptide link breaks, giving back the free amino acids. That is exactly what happens to a protein meal when you digest it.
beats.q1: Quick check. When two amino acids join by a peptide link, what is released?
beats.ends: [[chain]]Now look at the whole chain. Inside, it is a string of peptide links. But the two ends are different. [[n]]At one end, the first amino acid still has a free amino group. This is the N-terminal end. [[c]]At the other end, the last amino acid still has a free carboxyl group. This is the C-terminal end. [[read]]We always read a chain from the N-terminal end to the C-terminal end. In the middle of the chain, the amino and carboxyl groups are all used up in the links. Only the ends keep them free.
beats.seq: [[beads]]Here is a chain drawn the way the slide shows it, each bead coloured by its family of amino acids: arginine, aspartic acid, cysteine, leucine, isoleucine, tryptophan, and on. The body uses twenty standard kinds. [[order]]What makes one protein different from another is which amino acids it has, how many, and in what order. [[word]]It is like words made from an alphabet. The same letters in a different order make a different word. And even a chain of only four amino acids can be built in one hundred and sixty thousand different ways. That is our own arithmetic: twenty choices, four times over. Real proteins have hundreds of amino acids.
beats.roles: [[enz]]So what do all these chains do? First, enzymes. They speed up the reactions of the body, like the ones that digest your food. [[hor]]Second, protein hormones, which carry messages, insulin for example. [[hb]]Third, hemoglobin, the protein of red blood cells that carries oxygen. [[plasma]]Fourth, plasma proteins, the proteins dissolved in the blood. [[lipo]]Fifth, lipoproteins, which carry fats through the blood. [[ig]]Sixth, immunoglobulins, the antibodies that defend us against germs. [[struct]]And seventh, supporting structures: cartilage, bone, skin, nail and hair. Seven jobs from one kind of molecule.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which protein carries oxygen in the red blood cells?
beats.tree: [[chain]]Let us end by planting a tree. Here is our chain, with its N-terminal end and its C-terminal end. [[root]]It is the root. Every protein is a chain of amino acids, so every protein starts here. [[branch]]In the next lessons the tree grows three branches. Simple proteins are made of amino acids only. Conjugated proteins are a chain joined to a non-protein part. And derived proteins are the products formed when other proteins are broken down. [[dim]]We will visit them one at a time, simple proteins first. Keep this tree in mind.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]A protein is a complex nitrogen compound of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, sometimes sulfur, and it is a chain of amino acids. [[s2]]Amino acids join by the peptide link: the carboxyl group of one with the amino group of the next, and water is released. [[s3]]A chain has an N-terminal end with a free amino group, and a C-terminal end with a free carboxyl group. [[s4]]The order of the amino acids makes each protein different, and proteins work as enzymes, hormones, carriers, defenders and building material. [[end]]Now try the practice.
